title: lateinit, lazy, casts, numbers
scopeHtml: Scope: lateinit vs lazy vs nullable, lateinit internals and restrictions, is/as/as?, boxing and the Integer cache, numeric conversions, Char/String internals, type inference limits, and reflection-based parsers that break Kotlin null-safety. (Lazy thread-safety modes and Android property delegates are covered in the properties & delegation section.)

notes.title: Choosing between lateinit, lazy and nullable
notes.html:
The idea. Sometimes a property cannot get its value when the object is created: a view exists only after onCreateView, an injected dependency arrives after the constructor, a heavy object is only needed if the user opens a screen. Kotlin gives three honest ways to say "not yet", and they differ in who supplies the value, when, and what happens if you read too early.

The three options.

lateinit var val x by lazy { } var x: T? = null
Who supplies the value outside code (framework, DI, test setup), later the property itself, on first read anyone, any time
Mutable yes (var only) no (val only) yes
Type seen by callers non-null T non-null T T? (callers must check)
Read too early UninitializedPropertyAccessException impossible, computed on demand callers see null
Can go back to "absent" no no yes
Primitives (Int) not allowed allowed allowed (boxed)
Thread safety none SYNCHRONIZED by default none

How to choose, in one question: who knows the value?

  • Something outside the class fills it and it will definitely be there before use: lateinit. Examples: Hilt/Dagger field injection (@Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics in an Activity or Fragment, because the framework, not your constructor, creates those), lateinit var binding in a Fragment, @Mock lateinit var repo: Repo in JUnit/Mockito tests with a @Before that assigns.
  • The class can compute it but it is expensive or often unneeded: by lazy. Examples: a Moshi/Json instance, a compiled Regex, a SimpleDateFormat, val prefs by lazy { context.getSharedPreferences(...) } in an Application class. Cold-start-obsessed apps (Instagram, Facebook, Uber) push heavy singletons behind lazy so startup does not pay for work that may never be needed.
  • "No value" is a real state callers must handle (a user without a profile photo, a session that has not logged in): nullable.

lazy modes (details live in the delegation topic): SYNCHRONIZED (default, double-checked locking, thread-safe), PUBLICATION (several threads may compute, first published value wins), NONE (no locking, single thread only, e.g. main-thread UI code).

Real-life picture. You are moving into a flat. lateinit is a reserved parking spot with no car yet: "someone will park here before you need it". lazy is a coffee machine that grinds beans only when the first person asks for coffee, then keeps the cup ready. A nullable is a parking spot with an "EMPTY" sign that everyone must look at first.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking lateinit "to avoid ?." when absence is actually a valid state: you replaced a compile-time check with a runtime crash.
  • Saying lazy is "lateinit for val": the difference is that lazy initializes itself, lateinit is initialized from outside.
  • Forgetting that lazy captures its lambda (and whatever it closes over, e.g. a Context) until first access completes.

notes.title: What lateinit compiles to
notes.html:
The idea. The JVM has no concept of "a non-null field that has not been set yet". So Kotlin cheats: a lateinit property is an ordinary field that is secretly null, plus a getter that refuses to return null and throws a clear error instead.

Decompiled shape.

// lateinit var name: String
private String name;                       // plain field, starts as null

public final String getName() {
    String n = this.name;
    if (n == null) {
        Intrinsics.throwUninitializedPropertyAccessException("name");
    }
    return n;
}
public final void setName(String v) {
    Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(v, "<set-?>");
    this.name = v;
}

The thrown type is kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property name has not been initialized. It is a subclass of RuntimeException, so Crashlytics groups it under that name with the property name in the message, which is far easier to triage than a bare NullPointerException.

Field visibility is exposed. For a lateinit var, the backing field gets the visibility of the setter. A public lateinit var becomes a public Java field. That is deliberate: Dagger/Hilt field injection, Mockito @InjectMocks and Java reflection need to write the field directly without calling a Kotlin setter. A private lateinit var keeps a private field.

Cost. One null comparison per read, the same as any nullable read. It saves you typing ?. or !!, it does not make anything faster.

Local and top-level lateinit. Since Kotlin 1.2 you can also write lateinit var x: Foo as a local variable or top-level property (useful when a lambda assigns it before use).

Who sees the null. Kotlin callers always go through the checking getter. Anything that bypasses the getter sees the raw field: Java code reading the exposed field directly, reflection, and Gson (which writes and reads fields). So lateinit is safe only for Kotlin readers.

Real-life picture. An "under construction" sign on a shop. The shop is registered and the door exists, but if you walk in too early the staff stop you with a specific message instead of letting you fall through an unfinished floor.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "it is a non-null field": the field can be null at runtime, the getter hides it.
  • Claiming reflection-based libraries respect lateinit: they see a null field and do not throw.
  • Expecting UninitializedPropertyAccessException to be an NPE subtype: it is not, so catch (e: NullPointerException) will not catch it.

notes.title: lateinit restrictions and what to use instead
notes.html:
The idea. lateinit is only legal where "null means not initialized" can be represented safely. Each restriction follows from that single rule.

Not allowed Why Use instead
lateinit val it must be assigned after construction, so it must be reassignable val x by lazy { } or a constructor parameter
lateinit var x: Int (and Long, Boolean, Double...) a primitive JVM field cannot hold null, so there is no "unset" marker var x: Int = 0, or Int?, or by lazy
lateinit var x: String? null is already a legal value, so null could not mean "unset" plain var x: String? = null
lateinit with custom getter/setter there is no plain backing field for the null-check protocol normal property
lateinit in the primary constructor constructor parameters are set at construction, the opposite of "later" normal property

Important fine print: a value class wrapping a primitive is also a primitive underneath for this purpose, so lateinit var id: UserId is rejected when the underlying type is Long.

Industry examples. Room @Entity classes are tempting to write with lateinit var so a no-arg constructor exists; do not, give defaults or use constructor properties. Test classes use lateinit for mocks and the object under test. Android code uses lateinit var binding: ActivityMainBinding because the Activity constructor runs before setContentView.

What compile errors look like. "'lateinit' modifier is not allowed on properties of primitive types", "...of nullable types", "...on a property with custom setter". If you see them, the compiler is telling you null is not a safe sentinel.

Real-life picture. A "reserved" card on a restaurant table works only if a table can be empty. You cannot reserve a table that is bolted to the floor and always occupied (primitive), and you cannot put "reserved" on a table that already has a "free" sign meaning something else (nullable).

Common interview traps.

  • Explaining lateinit Int as a "Kotlin limitation": it is a JVM representation limit.
  • Reaching for lateinit on a val in tests: use by lazy or initialise in the declaration.
  • Forgetting that Delegates.notNull<Int>() is the standard workaround for a "late" primitive (it throws IllegalStateException if read early).

notes.title: isInitialized and why it is a code smell
notes.html:
The idea. ::name.isInitialized lets you ask "has this lateinit been set yet?" without risking the exception. It is a compiler-checked special form, not a normal reflection call.

class ProfileFragment : Fragment() {
    private lateinit var adapter: PhotoAdapter

    fun refresh() {
        if (::adapter.isInitialized) adapter.notifyDataSetChanged()
    }
}

Where you may call it.

  • Only on a property you can already access lexically: the same class, an outer class, or the same file for top-level properties.
  • Not from another class, not via an instance (other::adapter.isInitialized is rejected), and not for a property declared in a superclass.
  • The property must have its backing field visible at the call site, otherwise "this declaration is not accessible".

How it compiles. ::adapter.isInitialized is inlined to a plain null test on the backing field: this.adapter != null. No reflection object (KProperty) is created at runtime, so it is as cheap as any null check.

Why reviewers call it a smell.

  1. It admits you do not know whether the object is ready: the design has an unmodelled state. If "not ready" is a real state, a nullable or a sealed State is the honest type.
  2. It hides ordering bugs. A defensive if (::x.isInitialized) silently skips work when a callback arrives before setup, so the symptom becomes "sometimes nothing happens" instead of a crash you can fix.
  3. It is not thread-safe: another thread can initialise between the check and the use.

Legitimate uses. Idempotent setup (if (!::client.isInitialized) client = build()), cleanup in onDestroy where setup may have failed halfway, and test helpers. Even then, by lazy often says it better.

Real-life picture. Peeking into the parking spot to see whether the car is there. Fine once, but if you do it every morning, the real fix is to sort out why the car is sometimes not parked.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying isInitialized works on any property or from outside the class.
  • Using it as a replacement for lifecycle correctness: it masks the bug in Q023-style incidents.
  • Assuming it is atomic with the following use.

notes.title: lateinit and lifecycle-order crashes
notes.html:
The idea. Android creates, destroys and re-creates your Activities and Fragments in an order you do not control (rotation, process death, back stack, multi-window). A lateinit that is assigned in one callback and read in another is a promise about ordering, and the OS can break that promise.

Typical production incident (the Crashlytics top crash). A top crash group such as UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property presenter has not been initialized at onStart, at 0.3 percent of sessions, often concentrated on low-memory devices or on resume after the app sat in the background.

Common root causes:

  1. Assigned too late in the lifecycle. The field is set in onResume, but onStart (or a FragmentResultListener, an onActivityResult, a Compose LaunchedEffect) reads it earlier.
  2. Process-death restore. After the process is killed, the system re-creates the Activity and calls onRestoreInstanceState, restores Fragments from the saved FragmentManager state and runs their callbacks, before your "happy path" code that assigns the field in some onCreate branch (for example only when savedInstanceState == null).
  3. Fragment view lifetime. A Fragment's view is destroyed in onDestroyView while the Fragment instance lives on in the back stack. A lateinit var binding is not cleared, so it leaks the whole view tree; if you try to fix by recreating it conditionally you create ordering bugs.
  4. Async callback after destroy. A network response or Handler message touches a field that a teardown path replaced.

The standard pattern for view bindings:

private var _binding: FragmentFeedBinding? = null
private val binding get() = _binding!!           // valid only between onCreateView and onDestroyView

override fun onCreateView(...) = FragmentFeedBinding.inflate(inflater, container, false).also { _binding = it }.root
override fun onDestroyView() { _binding = null; super.onDestroyView() }   // LeakCanary: no leaked view tree

Also: use viewLifecycleOwner (not the Fragment) for observers, repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) to collect flows, and constructor/Hilt injection (assigned before any lifecycle callback) instead of manual assignment for dependencies.

How to reproduce. "Don't keep activities" in Developer Options, adb shell am kill <package> while the app is backgrounded, then reopen. Both exercise the restore path that QA's cold-start testing never hits.

Real-life picture. A cinema usher who expects the projector to be set up in the lobby, but on busy nights the audience is let in through the side door before the lobby routine runs.

Common interview traps.

  • Fixing the crash with isInitialized instead of fixing the ordering.
  • Not testing process death (only rotation).
  • Keeping lateinit var binding past onDestroyView (the leak LeakCanary reports as Fragment.mView retained).

notes.title: is, as and as?
notes.html:
The idea. Three tools answer "what kind of object is this?" with different confidence levels.

Operator Meaning If the type is wrong
x is T "are you a T?" returns Boolean (and smart-casts in the true branch) false
x as T "you are a T, treat you as one" throws ClassCastException (or NullPointerException if x is null and T is non-null)
x as? T "try to treat you as T" returns null 
val view = findViewById<View>(R.id.title)
if (view is TextView) view.text = "Hi"          // smart cast, no explicit cast
(view as? TextView)?.text = "Hi"                // safe cast + safe call
val tv = view as TextView                       // CCE if it is a Button

Runtime reality. is compiles to the JVM instanceof instruction; as to checkcast (plus a null check when the target is non-null); as? to instanceof followed by checkcast or null. All three are cheap, a few nanoseconds.

Edge rules.

  • null as String throws (the message says "null cannot be cast to non-null type kotlin.String"). null as String? is fine. null is String is false.
  • is on generic types: x is List<String> is a compile error (erased), only x is List<*> is allowed.
  • Smart casts require the value to be stable (val, local var not captured and modified, not a custom getter); otherwise the compiler asks for an explicit cast.
  • Prefer when (event) { is Click -> ...; is Scroll -> ... } for polymorphic handling, especially with sealed types.

Industry usage. RecyclerView adapters cast holder as FooViewHolder inside onBindViewHolder; Navigation Safe Args and Fragment result APIs use as? on arguments; analytics SDKs use as? on Intent extras because extras are Any?.

Real-life picture. is is glancing at someone's badge. as is shouting "Hello Doctor!" without looking, fine if right, embarrassing if wrong. as? is politely asking "are you a doctor?" and moving on if the answer is no.

Common interview traps.

  • Using as on data from outside your control (Intents, JSON Any, Bundle): prefer as?.
  • Thinking as? T can still throw: it cannot for type mismatch, but it can still be wrong for generics (see unchecked casts).
  • Expecting x is String on null to be an error.

notes.title: Unchecked casts and type erasure
notes.html:
The idea. Generics exist only at compile time on the JVM: List<String> and List<Int> are both just java.util.List at runtime (type erasure). So the runtime cannot check the type argument, and a cast like list as List<String> is only checked as list instanceof List. Kotlin marks it with the warning "Unchecked cast".

val raw: Any = listOf(1, 2, 3)
val strs = raw as List<String>      // compiles with a warning, does NOT throw here
val first: String = strs[0]         // ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String, HERE

The crash is far from the bad cast. The compiler inserts a checkcast String only when you read an element. The stack trace points to an innocent line, possibly in another module, possibly minutes later after the list went through a ViewModel and an adapter.

Why this matters.

  • Bundle.getSerializable, Parcelable lists, Map<String, Any> from JSON parsing, SavedStateHandle values and Intent extras are all Any-ish sources where unchecked casts are tempting.
  • With reified inline functions you can check the outer type (inline fun <reified T> Any.isA() = this is T), but still not nested arguments.

Safe alternatives.

  • Verify elements: raw.filterIsInstance<String>() or (raw as? List<*>)?.map { it as? String }.
  • Parse into typed models at the boundary (kotlinx.serialization, Moshi) instead of casting later.
  • If you must suppress, narrow the scope: @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") on the smallest expression and add a comment saying why it is safe.

Production symptom. Crashlytics shows ClassCastException: java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to java.lang.String in a view-binding or adapter class, with no as anywhere in the stack. Search the codebase for "Unchecked cast" warnings upstream.

Real-life picture. A sealed cardboard box labelled "fruit". The labeller (cast) only checks it is a box; the unpleasant surprise (a brick) appears when the customer opens it at home.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing as List<String> fails immediately.
  • Treating @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") as a fix.
  • Forgetting arrays are reified (Array<String> checks), unlike generic collections.

notes.title: Casting Context to Activity
notes.html:
The idea. context as Activity looks innocent and is one of the most common Android ClassCastExceptions. A Context is not always the Activity: it can be the Application, a Service, or a ContextWrapper around the Activity.

Why wrappers appear. Views inflated with a themed or wrapped context get a ContextThemeWrapper, not the Activity itself. Examples: AppCompat wraps contexts when it applies a theme overlay (android:theme on a view), Material components and MaterialAlertDialog do, Hilt's ViewComponent wiring uses a wrapper (ViewComponentManager.FragmentContextWrapper when a view is inside an @AndroidEntryPoint Fragment), and Compose's LocalContext can be a wrapper too.

Spot-the-bug scenario. A custom view cast getContext() as Activity for two years. After the screen moved from an Activity into a @AndroidEntryPoint Fragment, Hilt started wrapping the inflater's context in a FragmentContextWrapper: crash rate jumps to about 1 percent of opens on all OS versions and all devices. Crashlytics: ClassCastException: dagger.hilt.android.internal.managers.ViewComponentManager$FragmentContextWrapper cannot be cast to android.app.Activity.

The correct unwrap:

tailrec fun Context.findActivity(): Activity? = when (this) {
    is Activity -> this
    is ContextWrapper -> baseContext.findActivity()
    else -> null
}
// usage: context.findActivity()?.let { ... }

A ContextWrapper is a decorator holding the real context in baseContext; walking it is cheap (usually two or three hops). Compose helpers (LocalContext.current.findActivity()), Accompanist permissions and Navigation use exactly this loop.

Better design. Do not make views know about Activities: expose a callback (onCloseClicked), accept an interface, or have the Fragment/ViewModel handle navigation. If you need an Activity-scoped thing, pass it explicitly. Also never store the found Activity in a static or singleton (leak).

Real-life picture. A parcel can arrive inside several layers of wrapping paper. Assuming the first layer is the gift is the bug; you keep unwrapping until you hit the gift or run out of paper.

Common interview traps.

  • Using application or applicationContext as Activity (never an Activity).
  • Using getContext() of a view and assuming it equals the host Activity.
  • Showing a Dialog with an Application context (BadTokenException) because the unwrap returned null and was ignored.

notes.title: Int versus Int? and boxing
notes.html:
The idea. The JVM has two worlds: primitives (int, the number stored directly, 4 bytes, no object) and objects (java.lang.Integer, a heap object with a 12 to 16 byte header). Kotlin writes one name, Int, and the compiler decides which world to use.

What compiles to what.

Kotlin JVM
val x: Int (local, field, parameter, return) int
Int? java.lang.Integer (only an object can be null)
List<Int>, Map<String, Int>, Pair<Int, Int> Integer objects (generics are erased to objects)
Array<Int> Integer[]
IntArray int[]
(Int) -> Int lambda Function1<Integer, Integer>, boxing on each call (unless inline)

Bytecode of val a: Int? = 5 is Integer.valueOf(5); unboxing is intValue().

Memory numbers (64-bit ART/HotSpot, compressed refs). IntArray(1_000_000) is about 4 MB. A List<Int> of a million elements is an ArrayList of 1M references (4 bytes each with compressed oops) plus up to 1M Integer objects (16 bytes each), roughly 20 MB, and more GC pressure. Values -128..127 are shared via the Integer cache and cost nothing extra.

Where boxing bites in Android.

  • Big List<Int>/Map<Long, Item> in a ViewModel feeding a LazyColumn/RecyclerView.
  • Nullable numeric fields in hot data classes (val rating: Double? allocates a Double each parse).
  • Hot loops over (0 until n).map { ... } (boxed list) versus for (i in 0 until n) (compiled to a plain int loop).
  • Android's own answer: SparseArray, SparseIntArray, LongSparseArray, and androidx.collection primitive collections (IntList, MutableIntObjectMap, LongSparseArray).
  • Compose is built to avoid boxing: Dp, Offset, Color are value classes over primitives.

How to find it. Android Studio Memory Profiler allocation tracking (count of java.lang.Integer/Long), Perfetto/systrace GC events during scroll. Optimise only after measuring.

Real-life picture. Loose coins in a pocket versus each coin sealed in its own gift box before carrying: the boxed way takes more room, is slower to handle, and you must open every box to use the coin.

Common interview traps.

  • "Kotlin Int is always an object": it is a primitive whenever it can be.
  • Forgetting that List<Int> boxes even though Int is non-null.
  • Micro-optimising small lists: boxing only matters at scale or in hot paths.

notes.title: Integer cache and the === trap
notes.html:
The idea. == asks "same value?" (calls equals). === asks "same object in memory?". For boxed numbers, === gives different answers for the same value depending on a JVM cache.

val a: Int? = 127;  val b: Int? = 127
println(a == b)    // true
println(a === b)   // true  (both are the cached Integer.valueOf(127) object)

val c: Int? = 128;  val d: Int? = 128
println(c == d)    // true
println(c === d)   // false (two separate Integer objects)

Mechanism. Integer.valueOf(i) returns a pre-made object from IntegerCache for -128..127 (the upper bound can be raised on HotSpot with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, but ART uses the fixed default; confirm per runtime). Outside that range it allocates a new Integer. Long, Short, Byte and Char have similar caches (Long -128..127; Char 0..127); Float and Double have none.

Kotlin's guard rails. Identity comparison on a non-null Int is a compile error; on Int? it is a warning/deprecated ("identity equality for arguments of types Int? and Int? is deprecated"). That is why the example above uses Int?.

Why it survives in real code. Ported Java habits (if (id1 == id2) on Integer meant identity), Long ids from a JSON parser stored as Long?, and unit tests that use small ids (1, 2, 3 all hit the cache and pass) while production ids (millions) fail.

Always use == for numbers. Reserve === for identity of real objects, such as checking that a listener is the same instance you registered.

Real-life picture. A library keeps a shelf of pre-printed tickets numbered -128 to 127. Ask for ticket 50 twice and you get the very same ticket; ask for ticket 5000 twice and the clerk prints two different tickets with the same number.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying == and === are the same for Int.
  • Explaining the cache as "JVM optimisation of all numbers": only that range, and only via valueOf/autoboxing.
  • Writing tests with ids 1..3 that never expose the bug.

notes.title: Boxed identity bug in DiffUtil
notes.html:
The incident pattern. A notes app (600k DAU) uses ListAdapter with DiffUtil.ItemCallback:

override fun areItemsTheSame(old: Note, new: Note) = old.id === new.id   // id: Long?

With a 30-note seeded database in QA, ids are small, the Long cache returns the same object, === is true, everything works. Long-time users have ids in the thousands: === is false for every pair, so DiffUtil thinks every item was removed and a new one inserted on every update. Symptoms exactly as reported: the list flashes on each edit, scroll jumps to the top, swipe animations vanish (the ViewHolder is replaced, not moved), slow frames rise from 4 percent to 19 percent because every row rebinds. A release that also bumped RecyclerView and enabled R8 full mode sends engineers chasing the wrong cause; R8 neither caused nor hid it.

Why Long? was there. Room entities with autogenerated ids are Long?/Long = 0; JSON ids become Long?. Any Long? or generic Long is boxed.

Fix.

override fun areItemsTheSame(old: Note, new: Note) = old.id == new.id
override fun areContentsTheSame(old: Note, new: Note) = old == new        // data class equals

Prevention. Treat the warning "identity equality for Long? is deprecated" as an error in CI (allWarningsAsErrors or a specific -Werror rule), seed test databases with ids beyond 127 (use a real-sized fixture), and add a DiffUtil unit test with an id such as 1_000. The Android Studio Profiler shows rebind counts in this incident (thousands of onBindViewHolder calls for one edit).

Real-life picture. A cloakroom attendant who checks the physical ticket rather than the number printed on it: ticket 5 you hand in is accepted because it is the cached one, ticket 5000 is refused because the paper is a different copy.

Common interview traps.

  • Blaming the library bump or R8: reproduce with realistic data first.
  • Only testing with tiny seeded data.
  • Using === for ids because "ids are unique", conflating uniqueness with identity.

notes.title: Number conversions and literals
notes.html:
The idea. Kotlin has no implicit widening. val l: Long = intValue is a compile error, even though Java allows it. You must call toLong(), toInt(), toDouble() and so on.

Why Kotlin is strict.

  1. Boxed types would otherwise break equality: Int(1).equals(Long(1)) is false in Java, so a == b would stop meaning "same number" if one side were silently widened.
  2. Silent conversion hides precision loss and overflow bugs.
val i = 5
// val l: Long = i               // error: type mismatch
val l = i.toLong()
val f = 1 / 2                    // 0, integer division
val g = 1 / 2.0                  // 0.5
val big: Long = 5                // OK: an integer literal adapts to its expected type
val x = 3_000_000_000            // inferred Long, since it does not fit Int

Mixed arithmetic. Int + Long is allowed because operators are overloaded (Int.plus(Long): Long), and the result widens to the larger type. Int / Int is integer division (truncates toward zero). Int.toDouble() / n is needed for a real average.

Narrowing is silent and wraps. 3_000_000_000L.toInt() is -1294967296 (it keeps the low 32 bits). 300.toByte() is 44. Double.toInt() truncates and saturates (1e20.toInt() is Int.MAX_VALUE, NaN.toInt() is 0).

Literals. Suffixes L, f, u (unsigned, stable since 1.5), underscores (1_000_000), 0x/0b prefixes. Unsigned types (UInt, ULong) are value classes over the signed types.

Industry usage. Money: Stripe, Google Pay, Paytm APIs use integer minor units (paise or cents) as Long. Android sizes (File.length()), timestamps and byte counters are Long; view sizes and indices are Int; hence constant .toInt()/.toLong() at boundaries.

Real-life picture. Pouring from a big jug into a small glass: Kotlin makes you say so out loud, because some water will be lost.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting val x: Double = 1 to fail: literals are fine, variables are not.
  • Believing toInt() on an out-of-range Long throws.
  • Using Int for file sizes (breaks above 2 GB).

notes.title: Integer overflow in time math
notes.html:
The idea. Int holds up to 2,147,483,647. Arithmetic past that wraps silently to negative numbers: no exception, no log. Milliseconds are the classic victim because they are big.

val thirtyDaysMs   = 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000     // Int math: wraps to -1702967296
val thirtyDaysOk   = 30L * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000    // 2_592_000_000
val sevenDays      = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000      // 604_800_000, still fits (that is why 7 'worked')

Evaluation order matters: 30L * 24 * ... is Long from the first multiplication; 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1L overflows before the L joins. Only the compile-time constant case is flagged by lint in some versions, not variables from config.

Post-incident pattern. A news app reads cache_ttl_days from Firebase Remote Config. Default 7 works (604,800,000 fits). Product sets 30: ttlDays * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 wraps to a negative TTL, so now - cachedAt > ttl is true for every entry, the cache is considered expired on every read, QPS goes from 2.1k to 17k, the backend returns 429s, p95 load rises from 380 ms to 4.2 s. Rolling the remote-config value back repaired it. Nothing crashed, which is why overflow incidents are caught by dashboards, not Crashlytics. Fixes: Long/Duration everywhere (days.toLong().days, Duration.inWholeMilliseconds), Math.multiplyExact (throws ArithmeticException) at config boundaries, validation (coerceIn(1, 90)), and a test for the maximum allowed config value.

Related classics.

  • Year 2038: signed 32-bit seconds since 1970 overflow on 19 Jan 2038. Old SQLite columns, protocols and some Android code store seconds in an Int.
  • System.currentTimeMillis() is about 1.7 x 10^12, far beyond Int range; never .toInt() it.
  • Adding to Int.MAX_VALUE in counters (view counts, byte totals).
  • Floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. Never use Double for money.

Safe tools. Math.addExact/multiplyExact or Kotlin's Math.toIntExact, Long, java.time.Instant/Duration (API 26 or desugared), BigInteger/BigDecimal.

Real-life picture. A car odometer rolling from 999,999 to 000,000: it silently shows a tiny number and nobody warns you.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting the L on the last operand instead of the first.
  • Assuming overflow throws like in Python/Swift traps.
  • Testing only the default config value.

notes.title: Chars, Strings, templates and raw strings
notes.html:
The idea. A Kotlin String is an immutable sequence of UTF-16 code units, and a Char is one 16-bit unit, not one letter a human sees.

Internals.

  • String maps to java.lang.String. On ART with compact strings (Android 8 and later, confirm per version), Latin-1 text is stored 1 byte per char, other text 2 bytes.
  • Char is a 16-bit unsigned value (char primitive; boxed Char? is Character).
  • Strings are interned in a pool for literals; == compares content, === compares identity (two equal runtime strings are usually not ===).

Templates. "Hello $name, total ${price * qty}" compiles to StringBuilder.append(...) chains (or invokedynamic string concat when targeting JVM 9+, which Android does not use). In a loop, repeated + creates a new string per iteration (O(n squared)); use buildString { }.

Raw strings. """ ... """ keeps newlines and ignores escapes; use trimIndent() / trimMargin(). A $ still starts a template; write ${'$'} for a literal dollar sign. Good for SQL, JSON fixtures and regexes.

Locale traps.

  • String.format("%.2f", x) is locale-sensitive: it prints 1,50 in German/French locales. Use Locale.US/Locale.ROOT for machine text and NumberFormat/DecimalFormat for human text.
  • "title".uppercase() in a Turkish locale turns i into dotted I (U+0130); keys such as "id" stop matching. Use uppercase(Locale.ROOT) / lowercase(Locale.ROOT) for identifiers (Kotlin's lowercase() already uses ROOT; the old toLowerCase() did not).
  • Case-insensitive compare: a.equals(b, ignoreCase = true).

Industry examples. Server-driven keys and HTTP headers must be normalised with Locale.ROOT; A well-known real bug class is toUpperCase() on Turkish-locale devices breaking enum valueOf. Banking apps use NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale) for display.

Real-life picture. Train carriages (UTF-16 units) versus passengers (letters you see): the counts differ, because some passengers need two seats.

Common interview traps.

  • "%.2f".format(x) for an API payload.
  • toUpperCase() without a locale on identifiers.
  • Concatenating with + in loops of thousands.

notes.title: Unicode length and safe truncation
notes.html:
The idea. There are three different "lengths" of text: UTF-16 units (String.length), Unicode code points, and grapheme clusters (what a user sees as one character). Server limits are often a fourth: UTF-8 bytes.

val s = "a😀"
s.length                          // 3  (a + 2 UTF-16 units for the emoji, a surrogate pair)
s.codePointCount(0, s.length)     // 2
"👨‍👩‍👧".length                       // 8 units: 3 emoji code points joined by 2 zero-width joiners
"é".length                        // 1 if precomposed (U+00E9), 2 if e + combining accent
s.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8).size // 5 bytes (1 for a, 4 for the emoji)

The failure. name.take(20) or substring(0, 20) can cut a surrogate pair in half, leaving a lone high surrogate that renders as ?, a box or crashes some native text code. It can also cut a family emoji into pieces, or strip a flag's second half. A spec "max 20 characters" with 40 percent of users using emoji names makes this a daily occurrence.

Ambiguous-requirement answer. Clarify with product: "characters" almost always means grapheme clusters. Implement with:

fun String.takeGraphemes(n: Int): String {
    val bi = android.icu.text.BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance()   // API 24+; java.text.BreakIterator also exists
    bi.setText(this)
    var end = 0
    repeat(n) {
        val next = bi.next()
        if (next == android.icu.text.BreakIterator.DONE) return this
        end = next
    }
    return substring(0, end)
}

java.text.BreakIterator is simpler but older and less accurate for complex emoji sequences; ICU (android.icu.*, API 24 and above) follows current Unicode segmentation. For notification previews, truncate by graphemes then append an ellipsis. For server limits, additionally check UTF-8 byte count. For EditText limits, InputFilter.LengthFilter counts UTF-16 units (it does at least avoid splitting surrogates in newer versions; confirm) so a "20 character" field may hold 10 emoji.

Industry examples. WhatsApp, iMessage and Instagram handle names/bios by grapheme counts; SMS segmentation switches from 160 GSM-7 chars to 70 UCS-2 chars when a single emoji appears, which silently triples SMS cost.

Real-life picture. Counting people in a family photo by counting seat belts: a toddler on a lap, a pair sharing a seat; the number of seats and the number of people differ.

Common interview traps.

  • Using length for UI limits and String.take for truncation.
  • Forgetting server byte limits (a 20-char Hindi or emoji name is up to 80 bytes).
  • Normalisation: "e + accent" and "e-acute" look equal but == says no; normalise with java.text.Normalizer (NFC) before comparing.

notes.title: Type inference limits
notes.html:
The idea. Kotlin infers a type from the right-hand side. It is excellent, but the inferred type may not be the one you meant, and some situations have nothing to infer from.

Surprises.

  • Mixed literals: listOf(1, 2.0) is List<Number> (really List<{Comparable<*> & Number}>), listOf(1, "a") is List<Any>. An if returning Int in one branch and String in the other is Comparable<*> & java.io.Serializable, an intersection type you cannot write.
  • Nothing to infer from: val x = emptyList() fails; val x = mutableListOf() fails; null alone is Nothing?.
  • Lambdas: val add = { a, b -> a + b } needs parameter types.
  • Recursion: a recursive function with an expression body needs an explicit return type ("type checking has run into a recursive problem").
  • Builder inference works for buildList { add(1) } but breaks on complex cases.
  • Platform types (String! from Java) are inferred as "maybe null"; val n = javaObj.getName() hides nullability. Annotate Java (@Nullable/@NonNull) or declare val n: String? = ....
  • Numeric literal inference: val x = 1 is Int, val y = 1L is Long, val z = 0x7FFFFFFFF is Long automatically.
  • Smart-cast loss: inference of var types after a reassign in a lambda.

When to write types anyway.

  1. Public API (functions, properties): fun fetch(): Result<User>. An inferred return type changes silently when you refactor the body, breaking binary compatibility. Kotlin's explicit API mode (-Xexplicit-api=strict) enforces it for libraries.
  2. Long chains where the type is not obvious from the line.
  3. To widen a type: val state: UiState = UiState.Loading so later assignments of other subtypes compile (MutableStateFlow<UiState>(Loading) is a common fix where inference would pick Loading).
  4. Compile times: heavy inference in huge expression bodies (large when, builder DSLs, Compose-heavy code) slows the compiler; an explicit type shortcuts it.
  5. Generics with variance: val list: List<Number> = listOf(1, 2) vs inferred List<Int>.

Real-life picture. A tailor guessing a customer's size by looking at them is right nearly always, but for a uniform that hundreds of people will wear (public API), he writes the size on the label.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing inference is "dynamic typing": types are fixed at compile time.
  • Leaving public return types inferred (and then changing the body).
  • MutableStateFlow(Loading) inferring MutableStateFlow<Loading> and failing to emit Content.

notes.title: Reflection parsers versus null-safety
notes.html:
The idea. Kotlin guarantees String is never null only for code the Kotlin compiler checks. Libraries that build your objects by reflection (Gson, Firebase getValue(Class), Jackson without the Kotlin module, Java serialization) write fields directly and know nothing about Kotlin's String vs String?.

Why it breaks.

  • A backend omits "email"; Gson leaves the field null even though the Kotlin type says String. The NPE appears later, far from parsing, when you call email.length (Intrinsics.checkNotNullExpressionValue or a plain NullPointerException).
  • Constructor defaults are ignored. Gson looks for a no-arg constructor. A Kotlin class with all-default parameters gets a synthetic no-arg constructor and defaults work; a class with at least one parameter without default has none, so Gson uses sun.misc.Unsafe.allocateInstance, which skips constructors and initialisers entirely: val retries: Int = 3 becomes 0, a List default becomes null.
  • R8 shrinking renames fields; without @SerializedName or keep rules, parsing silently produces nulls in release builds only.
  • Firebase Realtime Database / Firestore getValue(User::class.java) requires a no-arg constructor (all params defaulted) and does not enforce nullability.

Production incident pattern. An e-commerce app (Retrofit + Gson, 3M DAU) ships a release; a new crash group appears in the product list from one region: the backend returns "price": null or omits discount for that market. Crashlytics: NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null or Attempt to invoke virtual method on a null object reference inside the adapter. The fix is not in the adapter.

Better choices.

  • kotlinx.serialization and Moshi with codegen (KSP) understand Kotlin: a missing non-null field throws SerializationException/JsonDataException at the parse boundary with the field name; defaults are honoured; nulls follow the declared type. Square's Moshi docs and the kotlinx.serialization docs both recommend this.
  • Layered models: parse into permissive DTOs (nullable fields, Gson if you must), validate, then map into strict domain models with requireNotNull/?: return null. A bad item is dropped or reported, not allowed to crash the list.
  • Contract tests and @Keep/R8 rules for any remaining reflection models.

Real-life picture. A delivery driver who swaps parcels without opening them: reflection hands over whatever it finds, including an empty box, and the labels on your shelf (types) do not stop it.

Common interview traps.

  • "Kotlin makes NPEs impossible": true only inside Kotlin-checked code.
  • Not knowing that defaults are skipped when Unsafe allocates the object.
  • Testing JSON parsing only in debug builds, never with R8 enabled.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
lateinit, lazy, nullable. Choose by who supplies the value and whether absence is legal. lateinit var is a null field with a throwing getter (UninitializedPropertyAccessException); field visibility follows the setter, so DI and mocks can inject. Not allowed on val, primitives, nullable types, custom accessors. ::x.isInitialized is a cheap null check but usually signals a modelling or lifecycle problem. by lazy computes once (modes SYNCHRONIZED, PUBLICATION, NONE). Nullable is for genuinely optional state.

Lifecycle. Order-dependent lateinit crashes appear after process death and in restore paths; null out view bindings in onDestroyView using the _binding pattern; test with "Don't keep activities" and adb shell am kill.

Casts. is checks, as throws, as? returns null; generic casts are unchecked because of erasure and fail far from the cast. Never context as Activity: unwrap ContextWrapper via baseContext.

Boxing. Int is int unless nullable, generic or used in generic lambdas, where it becomes Integer. IntArray and primitive collections save memory. == for values; === on boxed numbers works only inside the -128..127 cache, a classic DiffUtil areItemsTheSame bug.

Numbers. No implicit widening; narrowing and overflow wrap silently. Time and sizes are Long (put the L on the first operand), money is integer minor units or BigDecimal. Validate remote config values.

Strings. UTF-16 units, surrogate pairs and grapheme clusters differ from length; truncate with BreakIterator, check UTF-8 byte limits, use Locale.ROOT for identifiers, buildString in loops.

Inference and reflection. Declare types on public APIs, recursion, and when widening is needed. Reflection parsers (Gson, Firebase) bypass null-safety and constructor defaults; prefer kotlinx.serialization or Moshi codegen, or parse into nullable DTOs and map to validated domain models.

Interview one-liners.

  • "lateinit is null inside and throws on early read; lazy computes once on demand."
  • "Int? and List<Int> box; IntArray does not."
  • "Never compare boxed numbers with ===; the cache hides the bug until ids exceed 127."
  • "Time is a Long and the L goes on the first operand."
  • "length counts UTF-16 units, not what the user sees."
  • "Gson does not know Kotlin is non-null."

questions.promptHtml: You have a property that can't be given a value in the constructor. When do you pick lateinit var, by lazy, or a nullable var x: T? = null?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you choose based on who initializes the value and when, rather than habit. It also shows whether you understand what failure each option produces.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start by asking who supplies the value. If something outside the class supplies it later, through an injector, a lifecycle callback or a test setup, I use lateinit var. I'm promising it gets set before first read, and if I break that promise I get a loud UninitializedPropertyAccessException. If the class can compute the value itself but it's costly or not always needed, I use val by lazy: it computes once on first read and caches. If "no value" is a real, valid state, such as no logged-in user or a view that was destroyed, I use a nullable type, so the compiler makes every caller handle it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The three options say different things about how the property behaves over time:

lateinit var val by lazy {} var x: T? = null
Who initializes External code, any time The property itself, on first get Anyone
Mutable Yes (var only) No (val only) Yes
Can it be "absent" again No (no un-set from Kotlin) No Yes, assign null
Read before init Throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException Runs the initializer Returns null; compiler forces handling
Types allowed Non-null, non-primitive Any Any
Runtime cost One field + null check in getter Delegate object + lambda object + (default) lock One field
Thread safety None SYNCHRONIZED by default None

How to decide:

  • The value has a known source at declaration time → lazy. The initializer is part of the declaration, so it can never be forgotten.
  • The value comes from outside, after construction (field injection with @Inject lateinit var, onCreate, @Before in tests) → lateinit. Using a nullable here pushes !! or ?. onto every access even though the value is always present once the class is running.
  • Absence is part of the domain → nullable. A lateinit that you "reset" by setting a dummy value, or that you guard with isInitialized everywhere, is really a nullable property in disguise.

A lazy lambda can capture this, so it can reach other members. That makes it a good fit for derived values (val formatter by lazy { DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(pattern, locale) }). It is a bad fit for anything tied to a lifecycle that ends before the owner does, because the cached value outlives that lifecycle. The Fragment-view case is in the delegation section.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: CartRepository
) : ViewModel() {
    // Derived, costly, always computable by the class itself -> lazy
    private val priceFormatter by lazy { NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.getDefault()) }

    // "No coupon" is a real state -> nullable
    var appliedCoupon: Coupon? = null
        private set
}

class CheckoutFragment : Fragment() {
    // Set by the framework/injector after construction -> lateinit
    @Inject lateinit var analytics: Analytics
}

// Broken: nullable used for an always-present dependency -> !! everywhere
class BadFragment : Fragment() {
    var analytics: Analytics? = null
    fun track() = analytics!!.log("x") // the NPE moves around instead of failing fast at the source
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using lateinit for state that really can be absent, then scattering if (::x.isInitialized) checks around.
  • Using lazy on a var. That doesn't compile, because lazy gives a read-only delegate.
  • Assuming lateinit is thread-safe. It is a plain field, with no publication guarantees across threads.
  • Holding a lifecycle-scoped object such as a View, Context or binding in lazy on a longer-lived owner. The cached value leaks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can lazy be reset? → No. The stdlib Lazy has no reset. If you need resettable caching, write a small holder yourself or use a nullable field with a getter that fills it.
  2. What does lazy cost compared with lateinit? → A Lazy object, the lambda object, and a lock object for SYNCHRONIZED mode, plus a volatile read on every access. lateinit is just a field and a null check. The difference only matters in hot paths or on objects you create in very large numbers.
  3. Which would you use for a dependency in a class you control? → Neither. I'd use constructor injection with a private val. lateinit is for classes the framework instantiates (Activities, Fragments, Services) where you can't own the constructor.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer stops at "lateinit is var, lazy is val". A senior answer explains the choice in terms of who owns initialization and which failure you want: a loud crash at the source, guaranteed initialization, or forced null-handling. They also point out that constructor injection removes most uses of lateinit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that turned every lateinit into T? "to be safe" swapped one clear crash for dozens of !! NPEs that fired far from the real cause, and their crash-group count went up.

questions.promptHtml: What does a lateinit var compile to on the JVM, and what exactly happens when you read one that hasn't been set?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you can reason at the bytecode level, and whether you know how lateinit behaves from Java and from DI frameworks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A lateinit var compiles to a normal nullable JVM reference field, with null meaning "not set yet". The getter checks that field. If it's null, the getter calls Intrinsics.throwUninitializedPropertyAccessException with the property name, which throws kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property x has not been initialized. The setter has no check. One unusual detail: the backing field is exposed to Java with the same visibility as the property's setter. That is what lets Dagger/Hilt write @Inject lateinit var fields directly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decompiled shape (simplified) for class A { lateinit var name: String }:

public final class A {
    public String name;                       // field visibility == setter visibility

    public final String getName() {
        String v = this.name;
        if (v != null) return v;
        Intrinsics.throwUninitializedPropertyAccessException("name");
        return null; // unreachable
    }

    public final void setName(String v) {
        Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(v, "<set-?>");   // can't set null from Java either
        this.name = v;
    }
}

What follows from this:

  1. The check runs on every access through the getter. Inside the class, Kotlin still reads through the accessor logic, so even internal reads are checked. The check is one compare plus a branch the CPU predicts well, so it costs almost nothing.
  2. Setting null is rejected by the generated parameter null check, which throws NullPointerException in Kotlin 1.4+.
  3. The field is visible to Java. Java code can read a.name directly, skip the check, and get null. Java or reflection can also write null straight into the field. That is how a lateinit can end up "un-initialized again".
  4. Annotations such as @Inject on a lateinit property are placed on the field by default, which is what Dagger needs. That is the reason lateinit exists in Android code at all.
  5. lateinit is allowed on member properties, and since Kotlin 1.2 also on top-level properties and local variables. A local lateinit var is checked when it is read.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Session {
    lateinit var token: String

    fun header(): String = "Bearer $token"   // throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException if unset
}

fun main() {
    val s = Session()
    runCatching { s.header() }
        .onFailure { println(it) } // kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property token has not been initialized
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the exception is an NPE. It isn't: UninitializedPropertyAccessException extends RuntimeException, so Crashlytics groups it separately and the property name appears in the message.
  • Assuming a private lateinit is truly private to Java. The field is private only if the setter is private, which a private property's setter is. With lateinit var x; private set, the field is private too.
  • Expecting lateinit to give memory visibility across threads. Without @Volatile or another happens-before edge, a thread can see a stale null and throw.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why expose the field at all? → So that injection frameworks and Java code can set it without going through Kotlin accessors. Field injection was the original motivation.
  2. Can you put @Volatile on a lateinit? → Yes, @Volatile lateinit var compiles and makes the field volatile. It fixes visibility but not check-then-act races.
  3. What does lateinit look like after R8? → R8 usually inlines the getter, so you get a field load, a null check and a call to the throw helper. The property name string stays in the message even when the field name is obfuscated, which helps when reading a crash.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "it throws if you access it early". A senior answer describes the null-sentinel field, the exception type and its message, the setter-visibility field exposure, and how Java or reflection can bypass the check.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crash dashboards often show UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property binding has not been initialized. Because the property name is in the message, it is one of the easiest crash groups to triage, as long as nobody wraps it in a generic catch.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't lateinit be used with Int, with nullable types, with val, or with custom getters? What do you use instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Each restriction follows directly from how lateinit is implemented. Candidates who explain the mechanism instead of memorizing the rules stand out.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every restriction comes from one design choice: lateinit uses null in the backing field to mean "not set". A primitive int field can't hold null, so Int, Long, Boolean and the other primitives are out. A nullable type would make null mean both "not set" and "set to null", so that is banned too. val is banned because the whole point is to assign the value after construction. Custom accessors are banned because the compiler generates the getter that does the check. For primitives I use Delegates.notNull<Int>(), or I rethink the design and use a nullable or a default value.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Restriction Reason
Not on primitive types (Int, Double, Boolean...) They compile to JVM primitives, which have no null. Boxing them would quietly change the field type and its cost.
Not on nullable types null is already taken as the "uninitialized" marker, so the two meanings would clash.
Only var You must be able to assign it after construction.
No custom getter/setter The compiler owns the getter because that is where the check lives.
Not in the primary constructor A constructor parameter is initialized by definition.
Type must not be an inline/value class over a primitive or nullable Same null-representation problem. The exact rules depend on the underlying type, so check your Kotlin version's diagnostics.

Alternatives:

  • var count: Int by Delegates.notNull(). It stores the value in a delegate object, and reading before setting throws IllegalStateException("Property count should be initialized before get."). The cost is one extra object per property plus a virtual call per access.
  • A sensible default (var retryCount = 0), if 0 is semantically fine.
  • A nullable Int?, if "not set" is meaningful. Accept the boxing.
  • Restructure so the value arrives through the constructor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import kotlin.properties.Delegates

class Player {
    // lateinit var volume: Int          // compile error: 'lateinit' modifier is not allowed on properties of primitive types
    var volume: Int by Delegates.notNull()

    // lateinit var nickname: String?    // compile error: not allowed on nullable types
    var nickname: String? = null
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Switching to Int? "because lateinit doesn't work". Every read then pays for boxing and unboxing, and callers must handle null.
  • Putting Delegates.notNull() on hot properties of objects created in large numbers. That adds one extra object per property per instance.
  • Assuming lateinit var s: String accepts "" as "unset". It doesn't: any non-null value counts as initialized.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Delegates.notNull() support isInitialized? → No. ::x.isInitialized only works on lateinit properties. With notNull you'd have to catch the exception or track state yourself.
  2. Can a lateinit have a generic type T? → Yes, if T is non-null (T : Any). With an unbounded T, the compiler rejects it because T could be nullable.
  3. Why not let lateinit Int box under the hood? → It would silently change the field type and its performance, and it would break the "field is exposed to Java" contract for something that looks like an int. The language designers chose an explicit error instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer lists the rules. A senior answer derives all of them from the null-sentinel design and picks the alternative based on semantics and cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An Int? "ID not loaded yet" field read in a scroll listener boxed on every frame. Changing it to a plain Int with -1 documented as a sentinel removed the allocations seen in Memory Profiler.

questions.promptHtml: How does ::x.isInitialized work, where can you call it, and why do some reviewers treat it as a code smell?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It looks like a small API, but the answer reveals lexical-scope rules, how the compiler intrinsifies it, and design judgment.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: this::x.isInitialized (available since Kotlin 1.2) returns whether the lateinit backing field is non-null. The compiler doesn't use reflection for it. It compiles straight to a null check on the field. That's why you can only call it where the backing field is lexically accessible: inside the declaring class, an outer class, or the same file for top-level properties. I treat frequent use as a smell, because a lateinit that needs checking is usually a nullable value in disguise.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Syntax: ::prop.isInitialized for top-level or local scope, this::prop.isInitialized for a member, and other::prop.isInitialized for a bound reference, which is still subject to access rules.
  • Compilation: the property-reference expression is replaced with this.prop != null on the raw field. No KProperty object is created and no kotlin-reflect is needed.
  • Access rule: the compiler reports an error ("Backing field of 'var x: String' is not accessible at this point") when you call it from a subclass in another file, from an extension function, or from another class. In each of those places the field is out of reach.
  • There is no inverse: Kotlin can't "uninitialize" a lateinit. Tear-down code therefore can't reset it, and the property stays pinned to the last value until the owner is garbage-collected.

Legitimate uses:

  • Idempotent cleanup: if (::player.isInitialized) player.release() in onDestroy, where creation was conditional.
  • Test teardown, when setup may have failed partway.

Smell indicators: the same property is checked in more than one or two places, it's checked in a getter, or a separate "isReady" flag duplicates it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class VideoActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private lateinit var player: ExoPlayer

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        if (intent.hasExtra("url")) {
            player = ExoPlayer.Builder(this).build()
        }
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        if (this::player.isInitialized) player.release()   // OK: idempotent cleanup
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}

open class Base { lateinit var dep: String }
class Child : Base() {
    // fun check() = this::dep.isInitialized   // compile error: backing field not accessible here
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting it to work from a subclass or an extension. It doesn't. Expose a protected val isDepReady get() = ::dep.isInitialized from the base class if you really need it.
  • Using it to build a "check-then-init" lazy by hand on multiple threads. That is a race. Use lazy instead.
  • Writing ::x.isInitialized and forgetting the this qualifier on a member in an ambiguous context. It's usually fine, but this:: makes the intent clear.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it allocate a KProperty? → No. It is an intrinsic that compiles to a field null check.
  2. How would you release a lateinit to let GC collect it? → You can't through Kotlin. Make it nullable, or release the resource while keeping the reference (the owner's own lifetime then decides when it is collected).
  3. Is it thread-safe? → It's a plain field read. Without @Volatile it can return a stale false on another thread.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "it checks if lateinit was set". A senior answer explains the field-access intrinsic, the lexical restriction and its error, the lack of a reset, and when the check shows the property should be nullable.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Paired isInitialized checks spread across 9 call sites in a media screen kept out-of-date state alive across re-entries. Converting the property to a nullable with a single owner removed a class of "released player reused" crashes.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app has 2M DAU. A week after release 7.4, Crashlytics shows a new top crash at 0.35% of sessions:

Fatal Exception: kotlin.UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property cartPresenter has not been initialized
    at com.shop.MainActivity.getCartPresenter(MainActivity.kt:41)
    at com.shop.cart.CartBadgeFragment.onCreate(CartBadgeFragment.kt:28)
    at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.performCreate(Fragment.java:3094)
    ...
    at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentActivity.onCreate(FragmentActivity.java:...)
    at com.shop.MainActivity.onCreate(MainActivity.kt:55)

MainActivity.onCreate calls super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) on line 55 and assigns cartPresenter = CartPresenter(...) on line 58. CartBadgeFragment.onCreate does (requireActivity() as MainActivity).cartPresenter.attach(this). QA can't reproduce it on fresh launches. 80% of crashes come from devices with 3 GB of RAM or less. The release also bumped the Firebase SDK.
questions.promptHtml: What's going on, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap it in if (::cartPresenter.isInitialized)", or "make it nullable and use ?.". Either one hides the crash, and the badge silently never attaches. Blaming the Firebase SDK because the release bumped it is the red herring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does savedInstanceState tend to be non-null in the crashing sessions? Custom keys or breadcrumbs would show this, and it points straight at process-death restore.
    • When did CartBadgeFragment start reading cartPresenter in onCreate? Let's diff 7.3 against 7.4.
    • Are the crashes clustered on cold starts from recents? Process-state logs would show it.
    • Is the Firebase bump touching activity lifecycle at all? I want to rule it out quickly.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that moves the cartPresenter assignment to before super.onCreate if it doesn't depend on restored state. Or roll back the badge fragment's onCreate access through remote config, if a flag exists.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Process-death restore order. When the system recreates the Activity, super.onCreate(savedInstanceState) restores the FragmentManager, and restored fragments run onAttach/onCreate inside that call, before line 58. Low-RAM devices get process kills more often, which matches the device split. On a fresh launch, the fragment is added later, so the bug is invisible.
    2. Configuration change. This is the same mechanism, but it would also show up on high-RAM devices with rotation. It's less likely given the RAM skew.
    3. Firebase SDK. Nothing in the stack trace comes from it, so it's a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify each: I'd turn on Developer options → "Don't keep activities", or run adb shell am kill com.shop while the app is in the background and then reopen it from recents. That reproduces the crash deterministically. Breakpoints in MainActivity.onCreate and CartBadgeFragment.onCreate show the fragment's method running inside super.onCreate. A savedInstanceState != null custom key in Crashlytics confirms it in the field.
  5. Root cause: The fragment pulls a dependency from its host Activity in onCreate. During restore, fragment callbacks are dispatched from inside FragmentActivity.onCreate, so the host's lateinit isn't assigned yet. lateinit did its job: it failed loudly at the right place.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: assign the presenter before super.onCreate, if it doesn't need restored fragments or Activity state.
    • Long-term: remove the dependency on the host entirely. Put CartPresenter behind DI or a shared activityViewModels() ViewModel, which is created on demand and survives configuration changes:
    class CartBadgeFragment : Fragment(R.layout.cart_badge) {
    private val cartVm: CartViewModel by activityViewModels()

    override fun onViewCreated(view: View, savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                cartVm.count.collect { view.findViewById<TextView>(R.id.badge).text = "$it" }
            }
        }
    }
}
  7. Prevention: Run a "Don't keep activities" pass in the QA regression checklist. Add an instrumentation test that uses ActivityScenario.recreate(). Add a lint or review rule that forbids requireActivity() as SomeActivity dependency pulls in onAttach/onCreate.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't add isInitialized guards: the badge would silently stay broken and the crash would just move elsewhere. I also wouldn't make the presenter nullable with ?.attach, for the same reason. The ordering dependency is the bug, not the lateinit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not just move the line before super.onCreate?" → That works only if the presenter doesn't need anything super.onCreate sets up, such as restored ViewModels or the fragment manager. It is fragile, because the next dependency added to the presenter breaks it again.
  • "Would Hilt fix this?" → Yes for this crash. The generated Hilt_MainActivity injects at the very start of the onCreate chain. In recent versions it does this through an OnContextAvailableListener, which ComponentActivity.onCreate dispatches before FragmentActivity dispatches fragment onCreate. So @Inject lateinit var fields are already set when restored fragments run. Assignments in your own onCreate after super are not.
  • "How do you get the savedInstanceState signal into Crashlytics cheaply?" → setCustomKey("restored", savedInstanceState != null) in onCreate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team in this position "fixed" a similar crash with null checks, and checkout conversion dropped about 1% because a restored screen showed a stale cart. Reproducing it with "Don't keep activities" found the real ordering bug in 10 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests try/catch, isInitialized or nullable without explaining why it crashes. Blames the SDK.
  • Hire: Identifies process-death restore and the fragment-callbacks-inside-super.onCreate ordering, and reproduces it with "Don't keep activities".
  • Strong hire: All of the above, plus explains why low-RAM devices dominate, removes the fragment-to-activity coupling with a ViewModel or DI, adds recreate tests, and explains why Hilt injects before super.onCreate.

questions.promptHtml: Explain is, as, and as? in Kotlin. What does each do at runtime, and when would you use each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These are basic tools, but how you use them shows your error-handling habits and whether you rely on smart casts.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: is is a runtime type check that returns a Boolean. After it succeeds on a stable value, the compiler smart-casts the value, so I don't need an explicit cast. as is an unsafe cast: if the value isn't that type it throws ClassCastException, and casting null to a non-null type throws NullPointerException since Kotlin 1.4. as? is the safe cast: it returns null on mismatch. I usually pair it with ?: to supply a default or return early. I use when (x) { is A -> ... } for branching on types, as? at trust boundaries, and as only when a mismatch really is a programmer error and I want it to crash.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
On the JVM:

  • x is String → instanceof String.
  • x as String → checkcast String. If x is null and the target is non-null, Kotlin first emits an explicit null check, because checkcast lets null through on the JVM.
  • x as String? → a plain checkcast, which lets null through.
  • x as? String → instanceof and then either the value or null.
Expression x = "a" x = 1 x = null
x is String true false false
x as String "a" ClassCastException NullPointerException (1.4+)
x as String? "a" ClassCastException null
x as? String "a" null null

as? gives a nullable result, so x as? String has type String?. Writing (x as? String)!! is just as with a worse error message.

Generic types are checked only up to their class, because of erasure. That is covered in the generics section and in the next question.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
fun describe(x: Any?): String = when (x) {
    is String -> "string of ${x.length}"        // smart cast, no 'as'
    is Int    -> "int ${x + 1}"
    null      -> "null"
    else      -> "other ${x::class.simpleName}"
}

fun parseArgs(args: Bundle) {
    // Trust boundary: data may be malformed -> as? with a fallback
    val count = args.get("count") as? Int ?: 0
}

// Programmer error should crash loudly -> as
val host = requireActivity() as HostActivity

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing if (x is String) { (x as String).length }. The cast is redundant noise.
  • Using as? and then ignoring the null. That turns a bug into silent data loss.
  • Expecting as with a nullable source to throw a ClassCastException for null. Kotlin 1.4+ throws NullPointerException ("null cannot be cast to non-null type kotlin.String").
  • !is combined with an early return is the idiomatic guard: if (x !is Foo) return.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does is fail to smart-cast? → On mutable or open properties, custom getters, and properties from other modules. The compiler can't prove the value didn't change (see the smart-cast question in the type-system section).
  2. Is as free when the static type already matches? → The compiler removes upcasts and warns "No cast needed".
  3. How do you check x is List<String>? → You can't. Erasure means you write x is List<*> and check the elements yourself.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer gives the definitions. A senior answer maps each to bytecode (instanceof/checkcast), knows the null-cast exception type, and has a policy: crash on programmer errors, as? with handling at trust boundaries, and when/smart casts everywhere else.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sweep that replaced as with as? in deep-link parsing turned ClassCastException crashes into silently broken links. Fallbacks plus a logged non-fatal gave visibility without crashes.

questions.promptHtml: What is an unchecked cast in Kotlin? Why can a bad cast throw ClassCastException somewhere other than where you wrote as?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This separates people who've actually debugged heap pollution from people who just suppress warnings. It's at the boundary between casts and erasure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When you cast to a generic type such as as List<String>, or as T inside a generic function, the JVM can only check the raw class, or nothing at all for T. So the compiler warns "Unchecked cast" and emits little or no check. The wrong value passes through, and the ClassCastException appears later. It appears wherever the compiler inserted a concrete checkcast, which is usually where you first read an element as String. I treat every @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") as a debt that needs a justification comment. I prefer reified type parameters or explicit element checks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Erasure means List<String> and List<Int> are the same java.util.List at runtime. So:

val raw: Any = listOf(1, 2, 3)
val strings = raw as List<String>      // checkcast java/util/List -> passes
...                                    // value travels through 5 layers
val first: String = strings[0]         // compiler inserts checkcast String here -> ClassCastException

This is heap pollution: a variable whose static type is wrong about its runtime contents. The stack trace points at the read site, maybe in a different module or thread, not at the bad cast.

In a generic function fun <T> unsafe(x: Any?): T = x as T, there is no checkcast at all inside the function, because T erases to Any?. The check happens at the call site, where T is concrete, and only if the result is used as that type.

reified fixes the single-level case: inline fun <reified T> Any?.castOrNull(): T? = this as? T really checks T's class at the inlined site. It still can't check nested arguments: castOrNull<List<String>>() only checks List.

Null casts: null as String → NPE. null as T in a generic function where T is inferred non-null → no failure there, and the NPE appears at the first use. That is another failure that surfaces somewhere else.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
fun <T> Bundle.unsafeGet(key: String): T = get(key) as T   // no runtime check at all

fun demo(b: Bundle) {
    b.putInt("id", 42)
    val id: String = b.unsafeGet("id")   // CCE here, at the call site, not inside unsafeGet
}

// Safer: reified + safe cast, check happens where the type is known
inline fun <reified T> Bundle.getTyped(key: String): T? = get(key) as? T

// For collections: validate elements instead of trusting a cast
fun Any?.asStringList(): List<String>? =
    (this as? List<*>)?.takeIf { l -> l.all { it is String } }?.map { it as String }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Silencing UNCHECKED_CAST without validating. That just moves the crash to another place.
  • Believing reified checks generic arguments (List<String>). It checks only the outer class.
  • Using as T in a "convenience" helper that is used across the codebase, which spreads heap pollution everywhere.
  • Treating the CCE stack trace as the root cause and patching the read site with as?.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does Bundle.get(String) deprecation matter here? → Since API 33 the untyped getters (getParcelable(key), getSerializable(key)) are deprecated in favour of class-taking overloads (getParcelable(key, Foo::class.java)). The typed overloads let the framework check the class itself. Use BundleCompat for older API levels.
  2. How do you find the original bad cast? → Search for UNCHECKED_CAST suppressions and as T helpers on the value's path. Add a temporary eager check (require(list.all { it is String })) at the suspected cast and see if the crash moves.
  3. Can Kotlin warn you at the call site? → Only at the cast. With -Werror / allWarningsAsErrors, unchecked casts must be suppressed explicitly, so every suppression gets reviewed.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: A typical 3-YOE answer says "as throws if wrong". A senior answer explains erasure-driven deferred failure, where checkcast actually gets inserted, why the stack trace misleads, and gives a policy for suppressions plus reified/element validation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A generic SavedStateHandle wrapper with as T caused ClassCastException reports in an adapter two screens away. The root cause was a key reused with a different type after a refactor.

questions.contextHtml:
The profile screen used to be an Activity. It was migrated into a @AndroidEntryPoint Fragment inside MainActivity. The custom view below hasn't changed in 2 years. The day after release, the ClassCastException rate jumps from ~0 to 1.2% of profile-screen opens, on all OS versions. Pixel and Samsung devices are equally affected. The Compose-based settings screen, which uses a similar helper, shows a smaller but non-zero number of the same crash.

class AvatarView(context: Context, attrs: AttributeSet?) : FrameLayout(context, attrs) {
    private val host = context as AppCompatActivity

    init {
        setOnClickListener {
            host.supportFragmentManager.beginTransaction()
                .add(AvatarPickerDialog(), "picker").commit()
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun ShareButton() {
    val activity = LocalContext.current as Activity
    Button(onClick = { activity.startActivity(shareIntent()) }) { Text("Share") }
}
java.lang.ClassCastException: dagger.hilt.android.internal.managers.ViewComponentManager$FragmentContextWrapper
    cannot be cast to androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity
    at com.app.profile.AvatarView.<init>(AvatarView.kt:3)
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs, explain why they only showed up now, and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Change as to as?". The view then silently does nothing on tap. Or "pass the Activity into the view's constructor", which breaks XML inflation and the layout preview.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the fragment newly annotated with @AndroidEntryPoint? Does the 1.2% equal "profile opened from the new fragment entry point"? Where is ShareButton hosted: inside a Dialog, a ContextThemeWrapper, or a Hilt fragment's ComposeView?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the cast with a context-unwrapping helper (below). If a feature flag still routes to the old Activity, flip it back for affected users in the meantime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Context is a wrapper, not the Activity. A View's context is whatever context inflated it. Hilt @AndroidEntryPoint fragments return a FragmentContextWrapper from getContext(), and their LayoutInflater uses it, so every view inflated in that fragment has the wrapper as its context. Under the old Activity host, context really was the Activity, which is why the cast "worked" for 2 years.
    2. In Compose, LocalContext.current is the context of the hosting ComposeView. In a Hilt fragment it's the same wrapper. Inside a Dialog or under a themed wrapper it can be a ContextThemeWrapper. That explains the smaller number of crashes on the Compose screen.
    3. OEM-specific behaviour. This is ruled out because the crashes are evenly spread across manufacturers.
  4. How I'd verify each: In the debugger, check context.javaClass inside AvatarView.<init>. Walk (context as ContextWrapper).baseContext until you reach the Activity. Check the Crashlytics breadcrumbs for which host the crashing screen had.
  5. Root cause: Two unsafe casts that assumed Context is an Activity. The Android contract never promised that. A Context handed to a View or composable may be any ContextWrapper chain whose base eventually is the Activity.
  6. Fix:
